description: Test your knowledge of Pelvic wall and viscera.

cards.text: Name the three parts of the levator ani muscle and their primary action.
cards.answer: Pubococcygeus (supports viscera), puborectalis (maintains anorectal angle for continence), and iliococcygeus (elevates pelvic floor). All innervated by nerve to levator ani (S3, S4).

tip.tip: PPI: Pubococcygeus, Puborectalis, Iliococcygeus — three P's support pelvic function

cards.text: What is the relationship between the uterine artery and ureter, and why is this clinically important?
cards.answer: The uterine artery crosses the ureter 2 cm lateral to the cervix. This is remembered as 'water under the bridge'—the ureter must be identified and separated during hysterectomy to avoid iatrogenic ureteric injury.

tip.tip: 'Water under the bridge' — the ureter passes under the uterine artery at the cervix

cards.text: Define corona mortis and explain its surgical significance.
cards.answer: Corona mortis is an anatomical anastomosis between the obturator artery and inferior epigastric artery over the pectineal line. It is at risk during ilioinguinal approaches to hip/acetabular surgery, potentially causing massive hemorrhage if injured.

tip.tip: Corona mortis = 'crown of death' — dangerous vascular bridge at the pectineal line

cards.text: Describe the pathway of the internal pudendal artery from its origin to the perineum.
cards.answer: Arises from anterior division of internal iliac artery, exits pelvis via greater sciatic foramen below piriformis, courses around ischial spine, re-enters pelvis via lesser sciatic foramen, and supplies the perineum.

tip.tip: Internal pudendal does a 'U-turn' around the ischial spine — out and back in

cards.text: What are the branches of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery? (Use mnemonic)
cards.answer: OISVUIPI: Obturator, Inferior gluteal, Superior vesical, Vaginal/Inferior vesical, Uterine, Internal pudendal, Inferior epigastric (with Middle rectal as variable 8th).

tip.tip: OISVUIPI — think 'oil veepi' for the 8 anterior division branches

cards.text: What nerve damage during childbirth causes fecal incontinence, and what anatomical mechanism is lost?
cards.answer: Injury to the puborectalis muscle during childbirth causes loss of the 90° anorectal angle. This angle is essential for maintaining continence; its loss results in fecal incontinence.

tip.tip: Puborectalis creates a 90° 'bend' — damage = straight angle = incontinence

cards.text: Name the three major branches of the sacral plexus that exit the pelvis below the piriformis.
cards.answer: Sciatic nerve (L4–S3), posterior cutaneous nerve of thigh (S1–S3), and inferior gluteal nerve (L5, S1, S2). All exit below piriformis into the gluteal region.

tip.tip: Below piriformis: Sciatic, Posterior cutaneous, Inferior gluteal — the 'big three'

cards.text: What is levator ani syndrome and which population shows higher prevalence?
cards.answer: Levator ani syndrome is chronic pelvic pain caused by a hypertonic (tense) levator ani muscle. It is notably more common in South Indian women and presents with persistent pelvic discomfort.

tip.tip: Hypertonic levator ani = 'tight pelvic floor' syndrome — regional and gender variation exists
